flags.heading: Two Meanings of One Word
flags.text: In the broad sense, Scripture uses it for every believer in a state of grace — St. Paul greets whole congregations as “the saints,” meaning simply the holy people of God, still on the road.

flags.heading: Two Meanings of One Word
flags.text: In the narrower, more familiar sense, a capital-S Saint is someone the Church has formally recognized as already sharing the joy of heaven, whose life she holds up as a sure model.

flags.heading: Ask Them to Pray for Us
flags.text: This confidence rests on the Communion of Saints — the Church in heaven, the Church being purified, and the Church still on pilgrimage on earth, bound together as one body in Christ (CCC 946).

flags.heading: A Life Fully Given
flags.text: They ask to be imitated — not by repeating the outward details of their lives, but by making the same total gift of self to the same God who made them holy.

flags.heading: A Gathering With One Purpose
flags.text: It is an exercise of the teaching office Christ gave His Church — bishops in union with one another and, for the councils that bind the whole Church, in union with the Pope.

flags.heading: Who Can Call One, and What Makes It Count
flags.text: In the Church’s first thousand years, it was usually the Roman emperor who summoned an ecumenical council and paid for the bishops to travel — Constantine at Nicaea, Theodosius II at Ephesus, Marcian at Chalcedon.

flags.heading: What Councils Have Done
flags.text: Councils have also settled the Church’s most contested questions about who Christ is: Ephesus in 431 defended Mary’s title Mother of God against Nestorius, and Chalcedon in 451 defined that Christ is one Person in two natures, divine and human, ‘without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.’

flags.heading: Prepared For in the Old Covenant
flags.text: And at the center of the camp stood the Ark of the Covenant, carrying the manna and the tablets of the Law, the very glory of God dwelling, really and physically, in the midst of Israel.

flags.heading: Handed On, Not Invented Later
flags.text: St. Paul, writing to the Corinthians only about two decades after the Last Supper — earlier than any surviving Gospel — tells them plainly that he passed on what he himself received from the Lord.

flags.heading: Handed On, Not Invented Later
flags.text: He warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will answer for his body and blood, and that a believer who fails to discern the body eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

flags.heading: What the Miracles Are For
flags.text: Every account gathered elsewhere in this exhibition — a bleeding Host, a face seen in adoration, hosts that would not decay across centuries — is a sign offered to a faith that already stands on this older ground.

flags.heading: What the Miracles Are For
flags.text: They exist to help us recognize, again and again, what Scripture and the apostles and the Fathers have always taught: that Christ meant exactly what he said, and that he remains, truly, with us still.

name: Biblical Evidence for the Real Presence

flags.heading: The Words at the Supper
flags.text: The wording varies slightly between the three accounts, as eyewitness testimony recorded by different hands naturally does, but the claim itself never softens into something merely symbolic in any of them.

flags.heading: Answerable for the Body and the Blood
flags.text: Writing to the same Corinthians about receiving Communion carelessly, Paul warns that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup unworthily will have to answer for the body and blood of the Lord.

flags.heading: Answerable for the Body and the Blood
flags.text: Taken together, these four threads — the Supper narratives, Paul's early testimony, the Capernaum discourse, and Paul's warning about unworthy reception — form the biblical foundation beneath every account gathered elsewhere in this exhibition.

flags.heading: Substance and Accident
flags.text: Transubstantiation, in this account, is a change of substance without any change of accidents: the bread and wine's appearance, taste, and physical properties remain exactly what they were, while what they truly are changes completely.

name: The Church Fathers on the Eucharist

flags.heading: Irenaeus of Lyons, c. AD 180
flags.text: A bishop in Gaul who had heard St. Polycarp — himself a disciple of the apostle John — preach in his own youth, Irenaeus wrote at length against the Gnostic teachers of his day, who taught that the material world was fundamentally corrupt and unworthy of God.

flags.heading: Irenaeus of Lyons, c. AD 180
flags.text: Irenaeus turned the Eucharist itself into an argument against them: Christ, he wrote, was exhibiting to us His true flesh in the Eucharist, conferring on our own flesh the capacity for salvation.

flags.heading: Cyril of Jerusalem, c. AD 350
flags.text: Cyril told his catechumens not to judge by taste, since the senses report only bread and wine, but to hold with unwavering faith that they receive the Body and Blood of Christ.

flags.heading: Cyril of Jerusalem, c. AD 350
flags.text: Coming from a bishop teaching ordinary new believers rather than defending the faith to outsiders, his lectures show the doctrine was the Church's common, taught belief — not a specialist's private theory.

flags.heading: Sacrifices of a Little Apostle
flags.text: Her devotion centered, above every other object, on the Immaculate Heart of Mary; she sang of it, prayed to it, and begged that others be taught to love it as fiercely as she did.

flags.heading: Alone, for Love of Souls
flags.text: She bore it, by every account, without complaint, offering the pain the way she had once offered her lunch, for sinners, for the Pope, for the Immaculate Heart she loved so well.

flags.heading: Legacy: Love Like Jacinta
flags.text: Where her brother kept a silent vigil before the tabernacle, Jacinta could not stop speaking her love aloud, for Jesus, for His Mother, for every soul she feared might be lost.

flags.heading: A Boy of the Fields
flags.text: Francisco Marto was born on June 11, 1908, in Aljustrel, the sixth of seven children of Manuel and Olímpia Marto and older brother to Jacinta, not yet two when she arrived.

flags.heading: Held Under Threat, Then Vindicated
flags.text: By the final apparition that October, some seventy thousand people had gathered in a rain-soaked field to witness what became known as the Miracle of the Sun, Francisco among them, as quietly amazed as everyone else.
